Apple yesterday showcased what it described as "stunning evidence" derived from forensic analysis of a MacBook belonging to former employee Chang Liu, who has since joined OpenAI. The company accuses two ex-employees of stealing trade secrets related to hardware design and other areas.

The AI company swiftly hit back with legal filings, characterising the entire situation as a "mess of Apple's own making"…

The ongoing lawsuit seeks to determine whether Liu and Tang Tan misappropriated confidential information from their time at Apple to help OpenAI develop an AI hardware device. The complaint specifically notes that both engineers downloaded confidential engineering files after leaving the iPhone maker.

Apple was granted access to a MacBook belonging to Liu for forensic analysis to determine whether it contained evidence of illegal access to the company's intellectual property. Yesterday, the company filed court documents claiming to have uncovered four pieces of "stunning" evidence supporting its allegations.

According to Reuters, OpenAI's filings submitted the same day were equally uncompromising.

Specifically, it attributed the problems to three causes:

  • Apple encouraged employees to use personal iCloud accounts to access Apple documents
  • Departing employees were not given sufficient time to return company devices, hand over files, and complete handover procedures
  • Former employees would still be contacted by former colleagues for assistance after leaving, thus requiring access to company data

9to5Mac Commentary

On the surface, the evidence Apple submitted yesterday does appear quite compelling. OpenAI does not seem to deny that the company used information belonging to Apple, but rather argues that the iPhone maker failed to adequately protect such information.

However, while I am not a lawyer, as I understand it, this point could become a pivotal argument—because a company must first take reasonable measures to protect its data before it can claim that data constitutes a trade secret. If OpenAI can prove that Apple failed to do so, then even if the allegations of data being used are true, the AI company may still prevail.
